Lethargy
lĕth´ar-jy
n. (morbid drowsiness; dullness of spirit; the sleep that overtakes a soul with work to do)
Greek lethargia, from lethe, forgetfulness, and argos, idle. The forgetting and the idleness are joined in the word: a man grows dull because he has stopped remembering what is at stake.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lethargy is spiritual drowsiness. Paul makes the hour the argument: “knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed” (Rom 13:11). Proverbs presses the sluggard: “How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep” (Pro 6:9–10). In the parable, the wise virgins are no more awake than the foolish: “while the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept” (Mat 25:5). The call is a summons from the dead: “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Eph 5:14). And the Lord asks it personally: “Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?” (Mar 14:37).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines lethargy as morbid drowsiness; preternatural sleepiness; and dullness, inaction, inattention.

expand to see more

LETHARGY, n. Preternatural sleepiness; morbid drowsiness; continued or profound sleep, from which a person can scarcely be awaked.

2. Dullness; inaction; inattention.

LETHARGIC, a. Preternaturally inclined to sleep; drowsy; dull; heavy.

Key Scripture

Rom 13:11 — "And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed."

Pro 6:9 — "How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?"

Mat 25:5 — "While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept."

Eph 5:14 — "Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light."

Mar 14:37 — "And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?"

Modern Corruption

Spiritual dullness is mistaken for peace, and the sluggard's own account of himself is always that a little more sleep is reasonable.

expand to see more

Proverbs 6:10 is the sluggard's inner monologue reproduced exactly, and its power is in the diminutives: yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands. Nothing in it is a decision to waste a life. Each instalment is small, defensible and temporary, and the ruin described in the next verse arrives as a traveller — steadily, on its own schedule, without being invited. That is the mechanism of spiritual decline in most Christians. Almost no one resolves to drift; they postpone, in small units, for reasons that are individually sound.

Matthew 25:5 removes the comfort of comparison, and it is the detail preachers most often skip: they all slumbered and slept. Both parties. The wise virgins were no more alert than the foolish, and the difference between them was not vigilance in the night but oil bought beforehand. The parable therefore refuses to make watchfulness a matter of maintaining a constant emotional intensity, which no one can do; it makes it a matter of preparation made while there was time.

Mark 14:37 is the tenderest and most searching of these texts. Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? — and the Lord adds, the spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak, which is a diagnosis rather than an excuse and comes from the One who knows exactly how weak. Ephesians 5:14 supplies the only remedy that ever works: awake, arise, and Christ shall give thee light. A sleeper cannot rouse himself by resolution; the command is issued with the promise attached, and the light comes from outside the man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hupnos (G5258), sleep; gregoreo (G1127), to watch, stay awake; nustazo (G3573), to nod, slumber; Hebrew atsel (H6102), sluggard.

expand to see more

Greek ex hupnou egerthenai (G5258) — to awake out of sleep; Romans 13:11.

Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to watch; Mark 14:34–38, Matthew 25:13, 1 Thessalonians 5:6, 1 Peter 5:8.

Hebrew atsel (H6102) — sluggard; Proverbs 6:6–9, 13:4, 20:4, 26:14–16.

Usage

"“A little sleep, a little slumber” — each instalment defensible."

"“They all slumbered and slept” — both parties, and the oil was the difference."

"“Awake… and Christ shall give thee light” — the promise is attached."
